title: A Short Note on Convexity
text:
Let \(f\colon I\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex on an interval \(I\). For \(x,y\in I\) and \(t\in[0,1]\),
\[
f\bigl(tx+(1-t)y\bigr)
\leq
t f(x)+(1-t)f(y).
\tag{1}\]
Equation Equation 1 says that the graph of (f) lies below each of its chords.

Theorem 1 (Midpoint criterion) Suppose \(f\colon I\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuous and satisfies
\[
f\left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right)
\leq
\frac{f(x)+f(y)}{2}
\]
for every \(x,y\in I\). Then \(f\) is convex.


Proof. For dyadic \(t=k/2^n\), repeated application of the midpoint inequality gives Equation 1. Every \(t\in[0,1]\) is the limit of dyadic numbers, so continuity of \(f\) extends the inequality to all \(t\). This proves the claim.

The argument in Theorem 1 is a standard example of proving a statement first on a dense subset and then passing to a limit.

title: Compactness and Open Covers
text:
Definition 1 (Compact space) A topological space \(X\) is compact if every open cover of \(X\) has a finite subcover.

The definition in Definition 1 is purely topological. In Euclidean space it is equivalent to a more geometric condition.

Theorem 1 (Heine–Borel) A subset \(K\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) is compact if and only if it is closed and bounded.


Proof. Let \(K \subset \mathbb R^n\) be a compact set. Each point \(x \in K\) is included in some open ball \(B(x, r_x)\), thus: \[
K \subset \bigcup\limits_{x \in K}B(x, r_x)
\] By compactness, there are finite points \(x_1, \dots, x_M\) of \(K\) such that \(B(x_1, r_{x_1}) \cup \dots \cup B(x_M, r_{x_M})\) cover \(K\). We can show that this finite union of bounded sets is bounded.
Suppose \(\bar{K} \neq K\), and let \(x \in \bar{K} \setminus K\). By definition of the closure, there is some sequence \((x_i)_{i \in \mathbb N}\) fully included in \(K\) converging towards \(x\).

The distinction between compactness and sequential compactness requires care outside metric spaces. A standard treatment of compactness in metric settings can be found in Rudin (1976).

title: Compactness and Open Covers
text:
Definition 1 (Compact space) A topological space \(X\) is compact if every open cover of \(X\) has a finite subcover.

title: Compactness and Open Covers
text:
Compactness is a topological property

Theorem 2 Let \(f: X \rightarrow Y\) be a continuous function, and \(K \subset X\) a compact set. Then \(f(K) \subseteq Y\) is compact.


Proof. Indeed, let \(\bigcup\limits_{\lambda \in \Lambda} U_\lambda\) be an arbitrary open cover of \(f(K)\). \(f^{-1}\left(\bigcup\limits_{\lambda \in \Lambda} U_\lambda)\right) = \bigcup\limits_{\lambda \in \Lambda}f^{-1}(U_\lambda)\) contains \(K\). Thus, by compactness, there is some \(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_M\) such that \(K \in f^{-1}(U_{\lambda_1}) \cup \dots \cup f^{-1}(U_{\lambda_M})\), therefore: \[
f(K) \subseteq U_{\lambda_1} \cup \dots \cup U_{\lambda_M}
\]

title: Compactness and Open Covers
text:
Useful consequences

A continuous real-valued function on a closed bounded interval attains both its maximum and minimum. This is a simple consequence of Theorem 2.
if \(X \xrightarrow{f} Y\) is an injective continuous function, where \(X\) is precompact and \(Y\) is compact, then \(f\) is a homeomorphism onto its image (an immersion).

title: My mathematical journey
text:
Mathematics is a succession of a few enlightenments and very long phases of confusion. I truly wish the evolution of my mathematics had known somewhat of a more linear tendency, but it was rather highly irregular. When I look back however, some feelings from doing what we can reasonably call elementary maths are no different from what I still feel today despite my current topics of interests being slightly more advanced. I recall in this short story some moments of enlightenments that I claim to have provided me similar huge amounts of satisfactions.
age 8: Construction of \((\mathbb{Z}, +)\) : Breaking a universal rule of primary school maths
age 14: Neglecting physics lessons and finding out trigonometry is useful
age 16: Beating calculus
age 18: Set theory: embracing numberless maths
age 20: Metric space topology and the joy of living in \(\mathbb R^2\)
age 21: Gluing, pasting, cutting, counting holes: maths or playdough ?
Category theory: abstracting the abstractions
